Three strategies

Each strategy has its own rules. They are not blended into one score.

Strategy 1

Non-prime bargain, refurbish, sell

  • Any zone; not prime (house median below £1.53m)
  • London Plan future-growth score at least 0.3 (Opportunity Areas, town-centre upgrades, growth locations, industrial release, DLR extension, Great Northern Inner)
  • Refurbished exit price at most 10x local household income (FYE2023), so local buyers can carry it
  • Buy well below the street and sector sold median; check £/sq ft against local listings
  • Market capex £100/sq ft, 15% margin on total cost

WORKS ONLY AT AUCTION / DEEP DISCOUNT

Best areas: Ilford, Romford, Upminster, Mill Hill/Colindale, Woolwich, Sutton, Enfield Town. Of 73 screened houses none clears 15% at asking; two Romford auction lots clear it at guide.

Strategy 2

Prime bargain, refurbish, sell

  • Top 10% house prices (median at least £1.53m)
  • Resales that cleared costs in the area; listing £/sq ft below local median; not already refurbished
  • Market capex £200/sq ft; SDLT reaches 17% above £1.5m
  • Prime prices barely grew in 10 years (0.4–2.5% a year); profit comes only from the refurbishment gap

HARDEST

Best areas: Barnes, Queen's Park/Kilburn, Brackenbury, Fulham, Hampstead. Of 66 screened houses only two are within 15% of a viable price.

Strategy 3

Long-term rental hold, sell as investment

  • Houses only, nearest TfL station in Zone 1–3
  • London Plan future-growth score at least 0.3
  • Net yield on all-in cost at least 5% and positive cash flow after refinancing 75% at 5%
  • Regulation: Renters' Rights Act in force 1 May 2026 (no Section 21), EPC C by 1 Oct 2030 (£10k cap), selective licensing in several boroughs

THIN YIELDS

Zone 1–3 houses net about 4% on cost. Only room-let/HMO formats reach 5%+. Best areas: Canning Town/Custom House, Stratford, Forest Gate, Plaistow, Tottenham, Neasden.

What we corrected along the way

  • Flip uplift was gross. The +13.6% London resale uplift ignored SDLT, fees, finance and capex. With full costs a flip needs the exit at roughly 1.8–2x the purchase price.
  • Strategies were blended. The earlier "extension opportunity" score mixed plan, demand and cheapness. It is kept below for reference but does not drive decisions.
  • Slow past growth is not proof of potential. Weak areas can stay weak; rental hold now uses yields and rent growth instead.
  • Negative station premium is not a bargain signal. It often reflects main roads or smaller houses.
  • Plan-strong areas had the lowest yields. Great Northern Inner, Brent Cross and Hendon at 2.5–3.2% gross cannot be held on a mortgage.
  • Affordability. Walthamstow, Tooting, Earlsfield, East Dulwich and Harlesden exit at 12–20x local income and have almost no Plan growth, so they fail Strategy 1's rules.
  • Regulation was missing (Renters' Rights Act, EPC C 2030, licensing) and flats were excluded from Strategy 3 at your request.
  • Data limits: PTAL 2015 (pre-Elizabeth line), incomes FYE2023, small resale samples, asking £/sq ft from listings, sizes estimated where missing.

Opportunity screen: cheap now, strong future

Each of London's 1,002 neighbourhoods (MSOAs) gets a potential score from the Plan, TfL and constraint layers, and is compared with its median sale price. Move the sliders to change the weights; the map and list update. "Cheap" means below the London median price; "high potential" means top 40% potential.

#NeighbourhoodMedian price5-yr changePotentialMain driversWatch

Prices: ONS median price paid, year to Mar 2023 (39 neighbourhoods have no data). Transport access: TfL PTAL 2015, before the Elizabeth line opened, which is why the line gets its own bonus. Growth points are hand-placed from the Plan's figures.

Extension opportunity: buy a house, extend, hold

For buying terraced or semi-detached houses to extend. Combines how many such houses there are and how cheap they are, the premium a larger family house earns, planning feasibility, and steady growth. Large Opportunity Areas and student-heavy stations count against, because their demand is for flats and shared housing.

#NeighbourhoodScorePlan alignmentHouse median 2025Terraced + semiOvercrowdedPop. 2011–21Price / income10-yr a year2008–09 fallPrice trendWatch

House prices: ONS small-area medians 1995–2022 (year to December), extended with HM Land Registry sales 2023–2025, terraced and semi-detached combined by sales weight. Housing stock, families, overcrowding (bedroom occupancy −1 or worse) and age: Census 2021. Population change: ONS small-area estimates mid-2011 to mid-2021. Income: ONS small-area household income FYE 2020, so price/income uses 2025 house prices on 2020 incomes. Many boroughs have borough-wide Article 4 directions (often on shared housing or office conversions), so Article 4 carries a small weight; check what each direction covers.

Do big projects lift nearby houses? London evidence 1995–2025

For each project, neighbourhoods within 1 km are compared with neighbourhoods 3–9 km away in the same boroughs. The line shows the nearby price index divided by the comparison index (100 = moved the same), for houses and flats. Shaded band = from commitment to opening.

TypeCasesHouses: commit → openHouses: 5 yrs afterFlats: commit → openFlats: 5 yrs after

Figures are median extra growth a year, in percentage points, against the comparison area. Small samples: some projects have only 1–4 nearby neighbourhoods, and inner-London house medians rest on few sales, so single cases are noisy.

Sustained-demand screen: stations with a plan, room to grow and steady use

A station passes when its neighbourhood has a high Plan potential score, its 2019–2025 passenger growth is not yet high compared with other stations, and its use is steady through the year (no big summer dip from students or summer spike from tourists and events). Use 2025 TfL entry + exit taps. Office-dominated stations (weekend use under 55% of weekday) are excluded, because their weak recovery reflects hybrid working rather than untapped potential.

StationNearPotentialTaps 2025vs 2019Jul–AugWeekend / weekdayPrice rank

"Normal" Jul–Aug is the London median (about 9% below term-time months), so the band centres on 0.91. Growth percentiles compare stations with each other: London stations are on average still about 14% below 2019, so "low growth" here means below-typical recovery, not decline alone. Price rank 0 = cheapest neighbourhood. Station data: TfL Network Demand open data, daily taps 2019 to Sept 2026.
